subproblem.title: Composition (chain) rule for pointwise upper Lipschitz bounds
subproblem.statement: Let X, Y, Z be pseudometric spaces, f : X → Y, g : Y → Z, A ⊆ X, B ⊆ Y with f(A) ⊆ B, x ∈ X, and K₁, K₂ ∈ ℝ with K₁ ≥ 0 and K₂ ≥ 0. Assume (H1) for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(f(x′), f(x)) ≤ (K₁ + ε)·d(x′, x) for all x′ ∈ A with d(x′, x) < δ, and (H2) for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(g(y′), g(f(x))) ≤ (K₂ + ε)·d(y′, f(x)) for all y′ ∈ B with d(y′, f(x)) < δ. Then for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(g(f(x′)), g(f(x))) ≤ (K₁K₂ + ε)·d(x′, x) for all x′ ∈ A with d(x′, x) < δ. (In the language of the parent proof: if f is K₁-Lipschitz at x within A, f maps A into B, and g is K₂-Lipschitz at f(x) within B, then g∘f is K₁K₂-Lipschitz at x within A; x itself need not lie in A.)

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed proof p. 163 (“by (7), (8) and the chain rule”), in the pointwise form “6.1 Two rules (Composition)” of the parent proof; per the parent's erratum the a.e. bound on |Dψ| is replaced by pointwise upper Lipschitz constants.

1. Terminology. For a map h, a set S, a point p and K ∈ ℝ, say h is K-Lipschitz at p within S if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with d(h(p′), h(p)) ≤ (K + ε)·d(p′, p) for all p′ ∈ S with d(p′, p) < δ. Hypothesis (H1) says f is K₁-Lipschitz at x within A, (H2) says g is K₂-Lipschitz at f(x) within B, and the claim is that g∘f is K₁K₂-Lipschitz at x within A.
2. Fix ε > 0 and put η := min{1, ε/(K₁ + K₂ + 1)}. Since K₁ + K₂ + 1 ≥ 1 > 0 we have η > 0, η ≤ 1 and η·(K₁ + K₂ + 1) ≤ (ε/(K₁ + K₂ + 1))·(K₁ + K₂ + 1) = ε.
3. Apply (H1) with η in place of ε to get δ₁ > 0, and (H2) with η in place of ε to get δ₂ > 0. Since K₁ + η > 0, the number δ := min{δ₁, δ₂/(K₁ + η)} is positive.
4. Let x′ ∈ A with d(x′, x) < δ. Because d(x′, x) < δ₁, (H1) gives d(f(x′), f(x)) ≤ (K₁ + η)·d(x′, x). Because d(x′, x) < δ₂/(K₁ + η) and K₁ + η > 0, (K₁ + η)·d(x′, x) < δ₂. Hence d(f(x′), f(x)) < δ₂.
5. Since f(A) ⊆ B, y′ := f(x′) ∈ B, and step 4 shows d(y′, f(x)) < δ₂; so (H2) gives d(g(f(x′)), g(f(x))) ≤ (K₂ + η)·d(f(x′), f(x)) ≤ (K₂ + η)(K₁ + η)·d(x′, x), where the last step multiplies the inequality of step 4 by K₂ + η ≥ 0.
6. (K₂ + η)(K₁ + η) = K₁K₂ + η(K₁ + K₂ + η) ≤ K₁K₂ + η(K₁ + K₂ + 1) ≤ K₁K₂ + ε, using η ≤ 1, η > 0 and step 2. Multiplying by d(x′, x) ≥ 0 and combining with step 5: d(g(f(x′)), g(f(x))) ≤ (K₁K₂ + ε)·d(x′, x). As ε > 0 was arbitrary, the claim holds. ∎

Take δ₁ for f and δ₂ for g at level η; set δ = min{δ₁, δ₂/(K₁+η)}.
For x′ ∈ A with d(x′,x) < δ: d(f x′, f x) ≤ (K₁+η)d(x′,x) < δ₂, and f x′ ∈ B.
Apply the bound for g at f x: d(g f x′, g f x) ≤ (K₂+η)(K₁+η)d(x′,x).
(K₂+η)(K₁+η) = K₁K₂ + η(K₁+K₂+η) ≤ K₁K₂ + ε.

subproblem.title: Union rule for pointwise upper Lipschitz bounds over finitely many closed pieces
subproblem.statement: Let X, Y be pseudometric spaces, ι a finite type, G : ι → Set X a family of closed sets, B ⊆ ⋃_{k∈ι} G k, g : X → Y, y ∈ X and K ∈ ℝ. Assume that for every k with y ∈ G k and every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(g(y′), g(y)) ≤ (K + ε)·d(y′, y) for all y′ ∈ G k ∩ B with d(y′, y) < δ. Then for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d(g(y′), g(y)) ≤ (K + ε)·d(y′, y) for all y′ ∈ B with d(y′, y) < δ. (I.e. if g is K-Lipschitz at y within G k ∩ B for every piece G k containing y, then g is K-Lipschitz at y within B.)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X Y : Type) [PseudoMetricSpace X] [PseudoMetricSpace Y] (ι : Type) [Finite ι] (G : ι → Set X) (B : Set X) (g : X → Y) (y : X) (K : ℝ), (∀ k, IsClosed (G k)) → B ⊆ ⋃ k, G k → (∀ k, y ∈ G k → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ y' ∈ G k ∩ B, dist y' y < δ → dist (g y') (g y) ≤ (K + ε) * dist y' y) → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ y' ∈ B, dist y' y < δ → dist (g y') (g y) ≤ (K + ε) * dist y' y
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: rule “6.1 Two rules (Union)” of the parent proof. It replaces the printed a.e. reasoning at the point y = ψ^{(n+ℓ)}(x), which may lie on several closed (n + ℓ − 1)-faces of C, n := m + 1 (Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed p. 162: “let F be any closed (n+ℓ−1)-face of C which contains y”).

1. Fix ε > 0. For every k ∈ ι we choose r_k > 0 with the property (∗)_k: d(g(y′), g(y)) ≤ (K + ε)·d(y′, y) for all y′ ∈ G k ∩ B with d(y′, y) < r_k.
 (a) If y ∈ G k, the hypothesis applied to k and ε gives such an r_k.
 (b) If y ∉ G k, then y belongs to the open set X ∖ G k (G k is closed), so there is r_k > 0 with ball(y, r_k) ⊆ X ∖ G k. Then no y′ ∈ G k satisfies d(y′, y) < r_k, and (∗)_k holds vacuously.
2. Choose δ > 0 with δ ≤ r_k for every k: if ι is nonempty, the finite family k ↦ r_k attains a minimum at some k₀ (ι is finite), and δ := r_{k₀} > 0 works; if ι is empty, δ := 1 works vacuously.
3. Let y′ ∈ B with d(y′, y) < δ. Since B ⊆ ⋃_k G k, there is k with y′ ∈ G k; thus y′ ∈ G k ∩ B and d(y′, y) < δ ≤ r_k, and (∗)_k gives d(g(y′), g(y)) ≤ (K + ε)·d(y′, y). ∎

Formalization notes (non-binding): `Metric.isOpen_iff` applied to `(hG k).isOpen_compl` gives the ball in 1(b); `choose r hr hbound` over k; `Finite.exists_min r` (needs `Nonempty ι`) gives δ; `Set.mem_iUnion` for step 3.
proof_key_steps: For each piece G k pick a radius r_k: from the hypothesis if y ∈ G k, and a ball missing the closed set G k if y ∉ G k.
Take δ = min_k r_k > 0 (finite index type; δ = 1 if ι is empty).
Any y′ ∈ B within δ of y lies in some G k ∩ B with d(y′,y) < r_k, so the bound holds.

audit.reason: The exact pseudometric-space statement is proved: closedness supplies missing-piece exclusion radii, finiteness supplies a common positive radius, and the covering hypothesis supplies the applicable piece. Empty index types, empty pieces, arbitrary K, and y outside B are correctly accommodated.

subproblem.title: Radial retraction of a face of the unit cube onto its relative boundary, with its pointwise Lipschitz estimate (printed ψ_F and (8))
subproblem.statement: Let D ∈ ℕ, a ∈ ℝ^D = Eucl D with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, J a set of indices and c ∈ ℝ^D with c_i = a_i for all i ∈ J; write F := {x ∈ [0,1]^D : x_i = c_i for all i ∉ J} and |·| for the Euclidean norm. There is a map g : ℝ^D → ℝ^D such that for every x ∈ F with x ≠ c: (i) g(x) ∈ [0,1]^D; (ii) g(x)_i ∈ {0,1} for some i ∈ J; and (iii) there is s > 0 such that g(x)_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i, s·|x − c| ≤ √D, and for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |g(x′) − g(x)| ≤ ((1 + 4√D)·s + ε)·|x′ − x| for all x′ ∈ F with |x′ − x| < δ. (Informal remark, not part of the statement: when c is a face centre a_F, i.e. also c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J, such a g is the printed radial retraction ψ_F of F ∖ {a_F} onto the relative boundary of F, and s is the printed ratio t = |ψ_F(x) − a_F|/|x − a_F|.)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (D : ℕ) (a : Eucl D), (∀ i, 1 / 4 < a i ∧ a i < 3 / 4) → ∀ (J : Finset (Fin D)) (c : Eucl D), (∀ i ∈ J, c i = a i) → ∃ g : Eucl D → Eucl D, ∀ x : Eucl D, (∀ i, 0 ≤ x i ∧ x i ≤ 1) → (∀ i ∉ J, x i = c i) → x ≠ c → (∀ i, 0 ≤ g x i ∧ g x i ≤ 1) ∧ (∃ i ∈ J, g x i = 0 ∨ g x i = 1) ∧ ∃ s : ℝ, 0 < s ∧ (∀ i, g x i - c i = s * (x i - c i)) ∧ s * dist x c ≤ Real.sqrt (D : ℝ) ∧ ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ x' : Eucl D, (∀ i, 0 ≤ x' i ∧ x' i ≤ 1) → (∀ i ∉ J, x' i = c i) → dist x' x < δ → dist (g x') (g x) ≤ ((1 + 4 * Real.sqrt (D : ℝ)) * s + ε) * dist x' x
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed definition of the radial retraction ψ_F with origin a_F (p. 161) and printed (8) (p. 163), in the form of Section 2 of the parent proof ((N1)–(N3), (R1), (R4), (R5)); per the parent's erratum the a.e. derivative bound is replaced by a pointwise upper Lipschitz constant. Here c plays the role of a_F.

0. Preliminaries. For all i: a_i > 1/4 > 0 and 1 − a_i > 1/4 > 0, hence 1/a_i < 4 and 1/(1 − a_i) < 4. For p, q ∈ [0,1]^D, |p − q|² = Σ_i (p_i − q_i)² ≤ D because |p_i − q_i| ≤ 1, so |p − q| ≤ √D (fact (c4)). For every vector v and index i, |v_i| ≤ |v|.
1. Trivial case J = ∅. Then every x with x_i = c_i for all i ∉ J equals c, so no x satisfies the hypotheses and g := identity works. Assume from now on J ≠ ∅.
2. The gauge. For v ∈ ℝ^D and an index i put f_i(v) := max{v_i/(1 − a_i), −v_i/a_i}, and N(v) := max_{i ∈ J} f_i(v) (a maximum over a finite nonempty set; so f_i(v) ≤ N(v) for i ∈ J and N(v) = f_{i₀}(v) for some i₀ ∈ J). (N2): |N(w) − N(v)| ≤ 4|w − v|. Indeed |max{p, q} − max{p′, q′}| ≤ max{|p − p′|, |q − q′|}, so |f_i(w) − f_i(v)| ≤ max{|w_i − v_i|/(1 − a_i), |w_i − v_i|/a_i} ≤ 4|w_i − v_i| ≤ 4|w − v|; hence f_i(w) ≤ N(v) + 4|w − v| for every i ∈ J, so N(w) ≤ N(v) + 4|w − v|, and symmetrically N(v) ≤ N(w) + 4|w − v|.
3. Definition. g(x) := c + N(x − c)^{-1}·(x − c) for every x ∈ ℝ^D, with the convention 0^{-1} := 0 (so g(x) = c when N(x − c) = 0); for x ∈ F ∖ {c}, N(x − c) > 0 by step 4, and the values of g outside F ∖ {c} play no role. (When c is a face centre a_F, g is the printed radial retraction ψ_F of F ∖ {a_F} onto ∂F.)
4. Fix x ∈ F with x ≠ c and put v := x − c; then v_i = 0 for i ∉ J. As x ≠ c, some i₁ ∈ J has v_{i₁} ≠ 0; if v_{i₁} > 0 then f_{i₁}(v) ≥ v_{i₁}/(1 − a_{i₁}) > 0, and if v_{i₁} < 0 then f_{i₁}(v) ≥ −v_{i₁}/a_{i₁} > 0. Hence ν := N(v) ≥ f_{i₁}(v) > 0 (N3). Put s := 1/ν > 0. Then g(x) = c + s·v, i.e. g(x)_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i.
5. (i), printed (R1). For i ∉ J, g(x)_i = c_i + s·0 = c_i = x_i ∈ [0,1]. For i ∈ J we have c_i = a_i and f_i(v) ≤ ν: from v_i/(1 − a_i) ≤ ν we get s·v_i ≤ 1 − a_i, so g(x)_i = a_i + s·v_i ≤ 1; from −v_i/a_i ≤ ν we get −s·v_i ≤ a_i, so g(x)_i ≥ 0.
6. (ii). Choose i₀ ∈ J with ν = f_{i₀}(v). If f_{i₀}(v) = v_{i₀}/(1 − a_{i₀}), then ν·(1 − a_{i₀}) = v_{i₀}, so s·v_{i₀} = 1 − a_{i₀} and g(x)_{i₀} = a_{i₀} + 1 − a_{i₀} = 1. Otherwise ν = −v_{i₀}/a_{i₀}, so s·v_{i₀} = −a_{i₀} and g(x)_{i₀} = 0.
7. s·|x − c| ≤ √D, printed (R5). The centre c lies in [0,1]^D: c_i = a_i ∈ (0,1) for i ∈ J and c_i = x_i ∈ [0,1] for i ∉ J. By step 5 and step 0, s·|x − c| = |s·v| = |g(x) − c| ≤ √D. In particular s·|v| ≤ √D.
8. The estimate, printed (8) as (R4). Fix ε > 0, put β := 1 + 4√D > 0 and δ := min{ν/8, εν²/(8β)} > 0. Let x′ ∈ F with ρ := |x′ − x| < δ, and put w := x′ − c, so w − v = x′ − x. By (N2), N(w) ≥ ν − 4ρ > ν − ν/2 = ν/2 > 0. Put u := 1/N(w) > 0 and t := 1/ν = s.
 (a) g(x′) − g(x) = u·w − t·v = u·(w − v) + (u − t)·v.
 (b) u − t = u·t·(ν − N(w)), so |u − t| ≤ 4·u·t·ρ by (N2); and u < 2t because N(w) > ν/2.
 (c) |g(x′) − g(x)| ≤ u·ρ + |u − t|·|v| ≤ u·ρ + 4·u·t·ρ·|v| = u·ρ·(1 + 4·t·|v|) ≤ β·u·ρ, using t·|v| ≤ √D from step 7.
 (d) u = t + (u − t) ≤ t + 4utρ ≤ t + 8t²ρ, hence β·u ≤ β·t + 8βt²ρ ≤ β·t + 8βt²δ ≤ β·t + ε, since 8βt²δ ≤ 8βt²·εν²/(8β) = ε (t·ν = 1).
 (e) Therefore |g(x′) − g(x)| ≤ (β·s + ε)·|x′ − x| = ((1 + 4√D)·s + ε)·|x′ − x|.
9. Steps 4–8 establish (i), (ii) and (iii) for every x ∈ F with x ≠ c, with the single map g of step 3. ∎

Formalization notes (non-binding): obtain the gauge abstractly, e.g. `obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ : ∃ N : Eucl D → ℝ, ∀ v, N v = J.sup' hJ (f v)`, and use `Finset.le_sup'`, `Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup'`, `Finset.sup'_le`, `abs_max_sub_max_le_max`, `PiLp.norm_apply_le`; take `g := fun x => c + (N (x - c))⁻¹ • (x - c)`; the diameter bound follows from `EuclideanSpace.dist_eq` and `Real.sqrt_le_sqrt`; prove the vector identity (a) by `ext i; simp only [PiLp.add_apply, PiLp.sub_apply, PiLp.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul]; ring`.
proof_key_steps: Diameter of [0,1]^D is √D; the case J = ∅ is vacuous.
Gauge N(v) = max_{i∈J} max{v_i/(1−a_i), −v_i/a_i} is 4-Lipschitz (N2) and positive at v = x − c ≠ 0 (N3).
g(x) = c + (x − c)/N(x − c): ray identity with s = 1/N(x − c) > 0, g(x) ∈ [0,1]^D, and a coordinate in J attaining 0 or 1 (R1).
Pointwise estimate (printed (8)): |g(x′) − g(x)| ≤ βu|x′−x| with u = 1/N(x′−c) ≤ s + 8s²|x′−x|, giving ((1+4√D)s + ε)|x′−x| for |x′−x| < min{ν/8, εν²/(8β)}.

audit.reason: The gauge construction supplies one total map with every stated property. J empty is vacuous; existence of an admissible x establishes c in the cube without an additional hypothesis. The maximum gives a boundary coordinate, and the explicit positive radius controls the denominator and proves the exact pointwise estimate, including the unrestricted x′ quantifier.

subproblem.title: Similarity bound for the distance to La along rays from a face centre (printed (4)–(7), corrected)
subproblem.statement: Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. Let J be a set of indices, c, x, y ∈ ℝ^d and s ∈ ℝ with c_i = a_i for i ∈ J, c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J, x_i = c_i for i ∉ J, y ∈ C, s > 0 and y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i. Then min{1/4, s·dist(x, La)} ≤ dist(y, La), where dist(·, La) = infDist(·, La) is the Euclidean distance (equal to 0 if La = ∅).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m ℓ : ℕ) (a : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), (∀ i, 1 / 4 < a i ∧ a i < 3 / 4) → ∀ La : Set (Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), La = {y | ∃ J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ)), J.card = m + 2 ∧ ∀ i ∈ J, ∃ k : ℤ, y i - a i = k} → ∀ (J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ))) (c x y : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)) (s : ℝ), (∀ i ∈ J, c i = a i) → (∀ i ∉ J, c i = 0 ∨ c i = 1) → (∀ i ∉ J, x i = c i) → (∀ i, 0 ≤ y i ∧ y i ≤ 1) → 0 < s → (∀ i, y i - c i = s * (x i - c i)) → min (1 / 4) (s * infDist x La) ≤ infDist y La
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed displays (4)–(7) on p. 162 and the sentence “dist(y, L)/dist(x, p_F^{-1}(L)) = |y − a|/|x − a| by similarity” on p. 163, as corrected in the parent proof (similarity bound 6.2: the printed “|y − a| ≥ 3/4” is replaced by the bound min{1/4, t·d_a(x)}, and distances are measured to La itself, which adds Case 1 below).

Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. 

Put μ := min{1/4, s·dist(x, La)}. Recall that |p_i − q_i| ≤ |p − q| for every index i and p, q ∈ ℝ^d.
1. If La = ∅, then dist(x, La) = dist(y, La) = 0 by convention and μ = min{1/4, 0} = 0 ≤ 0. From now on La ≠ ∅; then dist(y, La) is the infimum of |y − w| over w ∈ La, so it suffices to show μ ≤ |y − w| for every w ∈ La.
2. Fix w ∈ La, with a set J′ of m + 2 indices and integers k_i such that w_i − a_i = k_i for i ∈ J′.
3. Case 1: some i ∈ J′ is not in J. Then x_i = c_i, so y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) = 0, i.e. y_i = c_i ∈ {0,1}. Since c_i ∈ {0,1} and k_i ∈ ℤ, either k_i ≥ c_i or k_i ≤ c_i − 1 (for c_i = 0: k_i ≥ 0 or k_i ≤ −1; for c_i = 1: k_i ≥ 1 or k_i ≤ 0). If k_i ≥ c_i then w_i − y_i = a_i + k_i − c_i ≥ a_i > 1/4; if k_i ≤ c_i − 1 then y_i − w_i = c_i − a_i − k_i ≥ 1 − a_i > 1/4. Either way |y − w| ≥ |y_i − w_i| ≥ 1/4 ≥ μ.
4. Case 2: J′ ⊆ J and k_i ≠ 0 for some i ∈ J′. Here 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1. If k_i ≥ 1 then w_i − y_i = a_i + k_i − y_i ≥ a_i + 1 − 1 = a_i > 1/4; if k_i ≤ −1 then y_i − w_i = y_i − a_i − k_i ≥ 0 − a_i + 1 > 1/4. So |y − w| ≥ |y_i − w_i| ≥ 1/4 ≥ μ.
5. Case 3: J′ ⊆ J and k_i = 0, i.e. w_i = a_i, for every i ∈ J′. Put w′ := c + s^{-1}(w − c). For i ∈ J′ ⊆ J we have c_i = a_i and w′_i = a_i + s^{-1}(a_i − a_i) = a_i, so J′ (with all integers 0) witnesses w′ ∈ La, and therefore dist(x, La) ≤ |x − w′|. For every index i, y_i − w_i = (c_i + s(x_i − c_i)) − w_i = s·x_i − s·c_i − (w_i − c_i) = s·(x_i − w′_i); hence y − w = s·(x − w′) and |y − w| = s·|x − w′| ≥ s·dist(x, La) ≥ μ.
6. The three cases are exhaustive, so μ ≤ |y − w| for every w ∈ La, and hence μ ≤ dist(y, La). ∎

Formalization notes (non-binding): split on `La.eq_empty_or_nonempty` (`simp` closes the empty case via `infDist_empty`); then `rw [Metric.le_infDist hne]`; the coordinate bound is `PiLp.dist_apply_le y w i` with `Real.dist_eq`; in Cases 1–2 use `le_abs.mpr`; in Case 3 build `w' := c + s⁻¹ • (w - c)`, prove `y - w = s • (x - w')` by `ext i` and `field_simp`, and finish with `Metric.infDist_le_dist_of_mem`, `dist_eq_norm`, `norm_smul`.
proof_key_steps: Reduce to |y − w| ≥ μ := min{1/4, s·dist(x,La)} for each w ∈ La (La empty is trivial).
Case 1 (a witness index of w is a fixed coordinate of the face): y_i ∈ {0,1} is > 1/4 away from a_i + ℤ.
Case 2 (a nonzero integer shift on a free coordinate): y_i ∈ [0,1] is > 1/4 away from a_i + k_i.
Case 3 (all shifts zero): w′ = c + (w − c)/s ∈ La and y − w = s(x − w′), so |y − w| ≥ s·dist(x,La).

audit.reason: The proof covers La empty and all three exhaustive witness cases. In the zero-shift case, the constructed w′ belongs to La and satisfies y − w = s(x − w′); positivity of s justifies scaling. Taking the infimum proves exactly the stated bound without unstated cube membership for x.

subproblem.title: Elementary facts on the dual skeleton La: closedness, face centres, cone property (printed (1), (2))
subproblem.statement: Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. Then: (1) La is closed; (2) for every set J of indices with |J| ≥ m + 2 and every c ∈ ℝ^d with c_i = a_i for all i ∈ J, c ∈ La; (3) for every set J of indices, c, x, y ∈ ℝ^d and s ∈ ℝ such that c_i = a_i for i ∈ J, c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J, x_i = c_i for i ∉ J, y ∈ C, s > 0 and y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i: if y ∈ La then x ∈ La. (Informal remark, not part of the statement: in (3), (J, c) describes a face of C with free coordinates J and centre c; (3) says that moving from x along the ray from the face centre to a point y of C does not create membership in La.)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m ℓ : ℕ) (a : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), (∀ i, 1 / 4 < a i ∧ a i < 3 / 4) → ∀ La : Set (Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), La = {y | ∃ J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ)), J.card = m + 2 ∧ ∀ i ∈ J, ∃ k : ℤ, y i - a i = k} → IsClosed La ∧ (∀ (J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ))) (c : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), m + 2 ≤ J.card → (∀ i ∈ J, c i = a i) → c ∈ La) ∧ ∀ (J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ))) (c x y : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)) (s : ℝ), (∀ i ∈ J, c i = a i) → (∀ i ∉ J, c i = 0 ∨ c i = 1) → (∀ i ∉ J, x i = c i) → (∀ i, 0 ≤ y i ∧ y i ≤ 1) → 0 < s → (∀ i, y i - c i = s * (x i - c i)) → y ∈ La → x ∈ La
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed proof p. 161, displays (1) and (2) (the segment from a to a_F lies in L_{k−1}(a), and L_{k−1}(a) is a union of translates of p_ℓ^{-1}(p_ℓ(a))), as facts 1(a), 1(b), 1(d), (d1), (d2) of the parent proof. Only 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 is used about a.

Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. 

1. (Integers in (−1, 1).) If k ∈ ℤ and −1 < k < 1 as real numbers, then k = 0.
2. (La is closed; fact 1(b).) For an index i let E_i := {y : y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ}, the preimage of the set ℤ ⊂ ℝ (the range of the cast ℤ → ℝ, which is closed in ℝ because the cast is an isometric closed embedding) under the continuous map y ↦ y_i − a_i; so E_i is closed. Directly from the definition, La = ⋃_{J : |J| = m+2} ⋂_{i ∈ J} E_i. Each ⋂_{i∈J} E_i is an intersection of closed sets, hence closed, and the union runs over the finitely many subsets J of the finite index set. A finite union of closed sets is closed, so La is closed.
3. (Face centres lie in La; printed (1), fact (d1).) Let |J| ≥ m + 2 and c_i = a_i for i ∈ J. Choose J′ ⊆ J with |J′| = m + 2. For i ∈ J′, c_i − a_i = 0, which is the integer 0. Hence J′ witnesses c ∈ La.
4. (Cone property; printed (2), fact (d2).) Let J, c, x, y, s be as in (3) and suppose y ∈ La, witnessed by J′ with |J′| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for i ∈ J′. We show x_i − a_i = 0 for every i ∈ J′; then J′ (with all integers equal to 0) witnesses x ∈ La.
 (a) No i ∈ J′ lies outside J. Indeed, if i ∉ J then x_i = c_i, so y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) = 0 and y_i = c_i ∈ {0,1}. If c_i = 0 then k_i = −a_i ∈ (−3/4, −1/4), so −1 < k_i < 0, impossible for an integer; if c_i = 1 then k_i = 1 − a_i ∈ (1/4, 3/4), so 0 < k_i < 1, impossible.
 (b) Let i ∈ J′; by (a), i ∈ J and c_i = a_i. Since 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 and 1/4 < a_i < 3/4, k_i = y_i − a_i lies in (−3/4, 3/4) ⊂ (−1, 1), so k_i = 0 by step 1, i.e. y_i = a_i. Then s·(x_i − a_i) = s·(x_i − c_i) = y_i − c_i = a_i − a_i = 0, and s > 0 gives x_i − a_i = 0.
5. Steps 2, 3 and 4 prove (1), (2) and (3). ∎

Formalization notes (non-binding): rewrite La as `⋃ J ∈ {J | J.card = m + 2}, ⋂ i ∈ J, (fun y => y i - a i) ⁻¹' Set.range ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ)` and use `Set.Finite.isClosed_biUnion (Set.toFinite _)`, `isClosed_biInter`, `Real.isClosed_range_intCast.preimage (by fun_prop)`; `Finset.exists_subset_card_eq` for step 3; step 1 by `exact_mod_cast` and `omega`.
proof_key_steps: An integer strictly between −1 and 1 is 0.
La is a finite union over |J| = m+2 of finite intersections of preimages of the closed set ℤ, hence closed.
A point agreeing with a on m+2 coordinates lies in La (face centres, printed (1)).
Cone property: a witness index of y ∈ La outside J would give an integer in (−3/4,−1/4) ∪ (1/4,3/4); inside J it forces y_i = a_i, hence x_i = a_i (s > 0).

audit.reason: All three conclusions match the prose. Closedness follows from finitely many closed integer-coordinate conditions; subset selection proves centre membership; the cone argument excludes fixed witness coordinates and forces the remaining integer shifts to vanish. It needs neither ℓ ≥ 1 nor x in the cube, consistently with the frozen type.

subproblem.title: Construction of the composite radial retraction ψ₀ = R^ℓ of C ∖ La: (α), translation property (β), and the structural properties (S1), (S2)
subproblem.statement: Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. Assume ℓ ≥ 1. There is a map ψ₀ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d such that (α) for every x ∈ C ∖ La, ψ₀(x) ∈ C and there is a set I of exactly ℓ indices with ψ₀(x)_i ∈ {0,1} for all i ∈ I; (β) for all x, x′ ∈ C ∖ La with x′_i − x_i ∈ ℤ for all i, ψ₀(x′)_i − ψ₀(x)_i = x′_i − x_i for all i; (S1): for every x ∈ C ∖ La for which there is a set I of exactly ℓ indices with x_i ∈ {0,1} for all i ∈ I, ψ₀(x) = x; and (S2): for every set J of indices with |J| ≥ m + 2, every c ∈ ℝ^d with c_i = a_i for i ∈ J and c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J, every x ∈ C ∖ La with x_i = c_i for i ∉ J, every y ∈ C and s > 0 with y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i, and such that y_i ∈ {0,1} for some i ∈ J: ψ₀(y) = ψ₀(x). (Informal remark, not part of the statement: in (S2), (J, c) is a face F of C of dimension |J| ≥ m + 2 with centre c = a_F, and y is the point where the ray from a_F through x leaves F, i.e. y = ψ_F(x), the radial retraction of F with origin a_F; so (S2) is the parent's ψ₀ = ψ₀ ∘ ψ_F on F ∖ La, and (S1) says ψ₀ fixes the points of C ∖ La lying on faces of dimension ≤ m + 1.)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ m ℓ : ℕ, 1 ≤ ℓ → ∀ a : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ), (∀ i, 1 / 4 < a i ∧ a i < 3 / 4) → ∀ La : Set (Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)), La = {y | ∃ J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ)), J.card = m + 2 ∧ ∀ i ∈ J, ∃ k : ℤ, y i - a i = k} → ∃ ψ₀ : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ) → Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ), (∀ x : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ), (∀ i, 0 ≤ x i ∧ x i ≤ 1) → x ∉ La → (∀ i, 0 ≤ ψ₀ x i ∧ ψ₀ x i ≤ 1) ∧ ∃ I : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ)), I.card = ℓ ∧ ∀ i ∈ I, ψ₀ x i = 0 ∨ ψ₀ x i = 1) ∧ (∀ x x' : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ), (∀ i, 0 ≤ x i ∧ x i ≤ 1) → x ∉ La → (∀ i, 0 ≤ x' i ∧ x' i ≤ 1) → x' ∉ La → (∀ i, ∃ k : ℤ, x' i - x i = k) → ∀ i, ψ₀ x' i - ψ₀ x i = x' i - x i) ∧ (∀ x : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ), (∀ i, 0 ≤ x i ∧ x i ≤ 1) → x ∉ La → (∃ I : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ)), I.card = ℓ ∧ ∀ i ∈ I, x i = 0 ∨ x i = 1) → ψ₀ x = x) ∧ ∀ (J : Finset (Fin (m + 1 + ℓ))) (c x y : Eucl (m + 1 + ℓ)) (s : ℝ), m + 2 ≤ J.card → (∀ i ∈ J, c i = a i) → (∀ i ∉ J, c i = 0 ∨ c i = 1) → (∀ i, 0 ≤ x i ∧ x i ≤ 1) → x ∉ La → (∀ i ∉ J, x i = c i) → (∀ i, 0 ≤ y i ∧ y i ≤ 1) → 0 < s → (∀ i, y i - c i = s * (x i - c i)) → (∃ i ∈ J, y i = 0 ∨ y i = 1) → ψ₀ y = ψ₀ x
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed proof p. 161 (with n := m + 1: the composite ψ₀ = ψ^{(n+1)}∘⋯∘ψ^{(n+ℓ)} of the radial retractions ψ_F and its translation property “ψ₀(z + x) = z + ψ₀(x)”), in the equivalent one-step form ψ₀ = R^ℓ of Step 3 of the parent proof, with the parent's (S1), (S2), Step 4 (α) and Step 5 (β). (S2) is stated with the exit point y of the ray from the face centre c = a_F through x; step 7 below shows that this y is R(x) = ψ_F(x) (or x itself if x ∈ ∂F).

Notation: m, ℓ ∈ ℕ, d := m + 1 + ℓ, indices i range over Fin d, ℝ^d = Eucl d with the Euclidean norm |·|, C := [0,1]^d (y ∈ C iff 0 ≤ y_i ≤ 1 for all i), a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, and La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and integers k_i with y_i − a_i = k_i for all i ∈ J}. For y ∈ ℝ^d let J(y) := {i : 0 < y_i < 1} (the carrier); |J(y)| ≤ d, and if y ∈ C and i ∉ J(y) then y_i ∈ {0,1}. Note a_i > 0 and 1 − a_i > 0. Call y active if y ∈ C, y ∉ La and |J(y)| ≥ m + 2.

1. Definitions. For y with J(y) ≠ ∅ let T_i(y) := max{(y_i − a_i)/(1 − a_i), (a_i − y_i)/a_i} and N(y) := max_{i ∈ J(y)} T_i(y) (N(y) := 0 if J(y) = ∅; that value is never used). Thus T_i(y) ≤ N(y) for i ∈ J(y), and N(y) = T_{i₀}(y) for some i₀ ∈ J(y) when J(y) ≠ ∅. Define R : ℝ^d → ℝ^d by: if y is active, R(y)_i := a_i + (y_i − a_i)/N(y) for i ∈ J(y) and R(y)_i := y_i for i ∉ J(y); if y is not active, R(y) := y. (For active y, R(y) = ψ_{F(y)}(y), the radial retraction of the carrier face F(y) with origin its centre.) Put ψ₀ := R^ℓ, the ℓ-fold iterate of R.
2. One step. Let y be active.
 (a) N(y) > 0. Otherwise every i ∈ J(y) has (y_i − a_i)/(1 − a_i) ≤ 0 and (a_i − y_i)/a_i ≤ 0, i.e. y_i = a_i; choosing J′ ⊆ J(y) with |J′| = m + 2 gives y_i − a_i = 0 ∈ ℤ on J′, so y ∈ La, a contradiction.
 (b) R(y) ∈ C. For i ∈ J(y): (y_i − a_i)/(1 − a_i) ≤ N(y) gives (y_i − a_i)/N(y) ≤ 1 − a_i, i.e. R(y)_i ≤ 1; and (a_i − y_i)/a_i ≤ N(y) gives (a_i − y_i)/N(y) ≤ a_i, i.e. R(y)_i ≥ 0. For i ∉ J(y): R(y)_i = y_i ∈ [0,1].
 (c) Let i₀ ∈ J(y) with N(y) = T_{i₀}(y). If N(y) = (y_{i₀} − a_{i₀})/(1 − a_{i₀}), then (y_{i₀} − a_{i₀})/N(y) = 1 − a_{i₀} and R(y)_{i₀} = 1; otherwise N(y) = (a_{i₀} − y_{i₀})/a_{i₀}, so (y_{i₀} − a_{i₀})/N(y) = −a_{i₀} and R(y)_{i₀} = 0.
 (d) J(R(y)) ⊆ J(y) ∖ {i₀}: R(y)_{i₀} ∈ {0,1}, and for i ∉ J(y), R(y)_i = y_i ∉ (0,1). Hence |J(R(y))| + 1 ≤ |J(y)|.
 (e) R(y) ∉ La. Let c ∈ ℝ^d with c_i := a_i for i ∈ J(y) and c_i := y_i for i ∉ J(y). Then c_i ∈ {0,1} and y_i = c_i for i ∉ J(y), R(y) ∈ C by (b), and R(y)_i − c_i = N(y)^{-1}·(y_i − c_i) for every i (for i ∈ J(y) both sides equal (y_i − a_i)/N(y); for i ∉ J(y) both are 0). By the cone property, part (3) of sibling skeleton_facts (with J := J(y), x := y, the point R(y) in the role of y, and s := N(y)^{-1} > 0), R(y) ∈ La would imply y ∈ La, which is false.
3. Iteration. Claim: for every k ∈ ℕ and every y ∈ C ∖ La, R^k(y) ∈ C ∖ La, and |J(R^k(y))| ≤ m + 1 or |J(R^k(y))| + k ≤ |J(y)|. Induction on k; k = 0 is clear. For the step let z := R^k(y) ∈ C ∖ La; note R^{k+1}(y) = R(z). If z is active, step 2 gives R(z) ∈ C ∖ La and |J(R(z))| + 1 ≤ |J(z)|; since |J(z)| ≥ m + 2, the induction hypothesis yields |J(z)| + k ≤ |J(y)|, so |J(R(z))| + (k + 1) ≤ |J(y)|. If z is not active then (as z ∈ C ∖ La) |J(z)| ≤ m + 1 and R(z) = z. Consequence: for y ∈ C ∖ La, taking k = ℓ and using |J(y)| ≤ d = m + 1 + ℓ, we get |J(ψ₀(y))| ≤ m + 1; so ψ₀(y) ∈ C ∖ La is not active and R(ψ₀(y)) = ψ₀(y).
4. (α) (parent Step 4). Let x ∈ C ∖ La and y := ψ₀(x). By step 3, y ∈ C and |J(y)| ≤ m + 1, so the complement of J(y) has at least d − (m + 1) = ℓ elements; choose a subset I of it with |I| = ℓ. For i ∈ I, y_i ∈ [0,1] ∖ (0,1) = {0,1}.
5. (β) (printed translation property; parent Step 5). Lemma: if y, y′ ∈ C ∖ La and y′_i − y_i ∈ ℤ for all i, then R(y′)_i − R(y)_i = y′_i − y_i for all i. Proof: if 0 < y_i < 1 or 0 < y′_i < 1, then the integer z_i := y′_i − y_i satisfies −1 < z_i < 1 (one of the two coordinates lies in (0,1) and the other in [0,1]), so z_i = 0 and y′_i = y_i. Hence J(y′) = J(y) =: J and y′_i = y_i for i ∈ J; consequently y is active iff y′ is. If neither is active, R(y′) − R(y) = y′ − y. If both are active, T_i(y′) = T_i(y) for i ∈ J, so N(y′) = N(y) (N(y′) = T_{i₁}(y′) = T_{i₁}(y) ≤ N(y) for a maximizing i₁ ∈ J, and symmetrically); then R(y′)_i = R(y)_i and y′_i − y_i = 0 for i ∈ J, while R(y′)_i − R(y)_i = y′_i − y_i for i ∉ J. Now let x, x′ ∈ C ∖ La with x′_i − x_i ∈ ℤ for all i. By induction on k, R^k(x′)_i − R^k(x)_i = x′_i − x_i for all i: k = 0 is trivial; for the step, R^k(x), R^k(x′) ∈ C ∖ La by step 3 and their difference is x′ − x ∈ ℤ^d by the induction hypothesis, so the Lemma applies. Taking k = ℓ gives (β).
6. (S1). Let x ∈ C ∖ La and I a set of ℓ indices with x_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∈ I. Then J(x) is contained in the complement of I, so |J(x)| ≤ d − ℓ = m + 1, x is not active, R(x) = x, and ψ₀(x) = R^ℓ(x) = x.
7. (S2). Let J, c, x, y, s be as in (S2). For i ∉ J, y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) = 0, so y_i = c_i.
 Case A: 0 < x_i < 1 for every i ∈ J. Then J(x) = J (for i ∉ J, x_i = c_i ∈ {0,1}), so x is active (x ∈ C ∖ La and |J| ≥ m + 2). We show N(x) = 1/s. For i ∈ J we have c_i = a_i and y_i = a_i + s(x_i − a_i) ∈ [0,1], so s(x_i − a_i) ≤ 1 − a_i and s(a_i − x_i) ≤ a_i, i.e. (x_i − a_i)/(1 − a_i) ≤ 1/s and (a_i − x_i)/a_i ≤ 1/s; thus T_i(x) ≤ 1/s for all i ∈ J and N(x) ≤ 1/s. Let i₁ ∈ J with y_{i₁} ∈ {0,1}. If y_{i₁} = 1 then s(x_{i₁} − a_{i₁}) = 1 − a_{i₁}, so 1/s = (x_{i₁} − a_{i₁})/(1 − a_{i₁}) ≤ T_{i₁}(x) ≤ N(x); if y_{i₁} = 0 then s(a_{i₁} − x_{i₁}) = a_{i₁}, so 1/s = (a_{i₁} − x_{i₁})/a_{i₁} ≤ N(x). Hence N(x) = 1/s, and R(x)_i = a_i + s(x_i − a_i) = y_i for i ∈ J, R(x)_i = x_i = c_i = y_i for i ∉ J; that is, R(x) = y. Therefore ψ₀(y) = R^ℓ(R(x)) = R^{ℓ+1}(x) = R(R^ℓ(x)) = R^ℓ(x) = ψ₀(x), by the consequence in step 3.
 Case B: some i₂ ∈ J has x_{i₂} ∉ (0,1); since x ∈ C, x_{i₂} ∈ {0,1}. First s ≤ 1: if x_{i₂} = 0 then y_{i₂} = a_{i₂} − s·a_{i₂} ≥ 0 forces s ≤ 1; if x_{i₂} = 1 then y_{i₂} = a_{i₂} + s(1 − a_{i₂}) ≤ 1 forces s ≤ 1. Next s ≥ 1: let i₁ ∈ J with y_{i₁} ∈ {0,1}; if y_{i₁} = 0 then s(a_{i₁} − x_{i₁}) = a_{i₁}, and s·x_{i₁} ≥ 0 gives s·a_{i₁} ≥ a_{i₁}, so s ≥ 1; if y_{i₁} = 1 then s(x_{i₁} − a_{i₁}) = 1 − a_{i₁}, and s·x_{i₁} ≤ s gives s(1 − a_{i₁}) ≥ 1 − a_{i₁}, so s ≥ 1. Hence s = 1, so y_i − c_i = x_i − c_i for all i, y = x, and ψ₀(y) = ψ₀(x).
8. Steps 4–7 prove (α), (β), (S1) and (S2) for ψ₀ = R^ℓ. ∎

subproblem.title: Claim (3) of Lemma 5.4: the bound c₁/dist(x, La) for every ψ₀ satisfying (S1) and (S2), by induction over face dimension
subproblem.statement: Let m, ℓ ∈ ℕ with ℓ ≥ 1 and d := m + 1 + ℓ. There is c₁ = c₁(m, ℓ) ≥ 0 such that for every a ∈ ℝ^d with 1/4 < a_i < 3/4 for all i, with La := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of indices with |J| = m + 2 and y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ for all i ∈ J} and C := [0,1]^d, and for every map ψ₀ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d satisfying (S1): for every x ∈ C ∖ La for which there is a set I of exactly ℓ indices with x_i ∈ {0,1} for all i ∈ I, ψ₀(x) = x; and (S2): for every set J of indices with |J| ≥ m + 2, every c ∈ ℝ^d with c_i = a_i for i ∈ J and c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J, every x ∈ C ∖ La with x_i = c_i for i ∉ J, every y ∈ C and s > 0 with y_i − c_i = s·(x_i − c_i) for all i, and such that y_i ∈ {0,1} for some i ∈ J: ψ₀(y) = ψ₀(x); the following holds: (γ) for every x ∈ C ∖ La and every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |ψ₀(x′) − ψ₀(x)| ≤ (c₁/dist(x, La) + ε)·|x′ − x| for all x′ ∈ C ∖ La with |x′ − x| < δ (Euclidean norm; dist(x, La) = infDist x La).

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4, printed claim (3) and its proof by induction on k (pp. 162–163, with n := m + 1: displays (4)–(8), “ψ = ψ̃ ∘ ψ^{n+ℓ}” and the chain rule), written as Steps 6.3–6.6 of the parent proof: induction over the dimension j of the faces of C inside ℝ^d with distances measured to La, with the parent's errata (similarity bound with constant 1/4 instead of the printed “|y − a| ≥ 3/4”; pointwise upper Lipschitz constants instead of a.e. bounds on |Dψ|). All properties of ψ₀ that are used are (S1) and (S2), which encode the printed facts that ψ₀ is the identity on the n-faces and that ψ₀ = ψ₀ ∘ ψ_F on F ∖ La.

0. Notation and constants. d := m + 1 + ℓ ≥ m + 2 ≥ 2; |·| is the Euclidean norm; C := [0,1]^d; d_a(x) := dist(x, La) = infDist(x, La). Put r := √d ≥ 1, β := 1 + 4r, q := 4rβ (so q ≥ β, as 4r ≥ 1), and for j ≥ m + 2, c₁(j) := β·r·q^{j−(m+2)} ≥ 0; thus c₁(m + 2) = βr and c₁(j + 1) = q·c₁(j). Set c₁ := c₁(d) ≥ 0; it depends only on m and ℓ, and is fixed before a. Say that a map h is K-Lipschitz at p within S if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |h(p′) − h(p)| ≤ (K + ε)|p′ − p| for all p′ ∈ S with |p′ − p| < δ; this persists if K is increased or S is shrunk.
1. Fix a, La and ψ₀ satisfying (S1) and (S2). By sibling skeleton_facts: La is closed; every c with c_i = a_i on at least m + 2 indices lies in La (in particular a ∈ La, using all d ≥ m + 2 indices, so La ≠ ∅); and the cone property (3) holds. Consequently d_a(x) > 0 for every x ∉ La (a point outside a closed nonempty set has positive distance to it), and d_a(x) ≤ |x − c| for every c ∈ La.
2. Faces and the claim. A face is a pair (J, c) with J a set of indices and c ∈ ℝ^d such that c_i = a_i for i ∈ J and c_i ∈ {0,1} for i ∉ J; its point set is F := {x ∈ C : x_i = c_i for all i ∉ J} and its dimension is |J|. Claim P(j) (m + 2 ≤ j ≤ d): for every face (J, c) with |J| = j and every x ∈ F ∖ La, ψ₀ is (c₁(j)/d_a(x))-Lipschitz at x within F ∖ La. P(j) is proved by induction on j.
3. Common setup for a face (J, c) with |J| ≥ m + 2. By step 1, c ∈ La, so every x′ ∈ F ∖ La satisfies x′ ≠ c. Let g be the map given by sibling radial_map for D := d, a, J and c. For x′ ∈ F ∖ La, radial_map yields: g(x′) ∈ C; g(x′)_i ∈ {0,1} for some i ∈ J; and some s′ > 0 with g(x′)_i − c_i = s′·(x′_i − c_i) for all i. Hence g(x′)_i = c_i for i ∉ J; g(x′) ∉ La (by the cone property, g(x′) ∈ La would imply x′ ∈ La); and by (S2), applied to J, c, x′, y := g(x′) and s′, ψ₀(g(x′)) = ψ₀(x′).
4. Base case j = m + 2 (printed: “(3) is evident from construction in case ℓ = 1”). Let (J, c) be a face with |J| = m + 2. For x′ ∈ F ∖ La choose i ∈ J with g(x′)_i ∈ {0,1}; the set I := {i} ∪ (indices not in J) has exactly 1 + (d − (m + 2)) = ℓ elements, and g(x′)_k ∈ {0,1} for k ∈ I (for k ∉ J, g(x′)_k = c_k ∈ {0,1}). Since g(x′) ∈ C ∖ La, (S1) gives ψ₀(g(x′)) = g(x′), so ψ₀(x′) = g(x′) by step 3. Now let x ∈ F ∖ La, with parameter s from radial_map. Given ε > 0, radial_map gives δ > 0 with |g(x′) − g(x)| ≤ (βs + ε)|x′ − x| for all x′ ∈ F with |x′ − x| < δ; for x′ ∈ F ∖ La this reads |ψ₀(x′) − ψ₀(x)| ≤ (βs + ε)|x′ − x|. Moreover s·d_a(x) ≤ s·|x − c| ≤ r by step 1 and radial_map, so βs ≤ βr/d_a(x) = c₁(m + 2)/d_a(x). This proves P(m + 2).
5. Induction step (the printed induction). Let m + 2 ≤ j < d, assume P(j), and let (J, c) be a face with |J| = j + 1 and x ∈ F ∖ La. Let y := g(x) and s > 0 its parameter, so y − c = s·(x − c), y ∈ C, y ∉ La and y_i = c_i for i ∉ J (step 3). Put A := F ∖ La and B := {y′ ∈ C : y′_i = c_i for all i ∉ J, y′_i ∈ {0,1} for some i ∈ J, y′ ∉ La} (= ∂F ∖ La). For each index i and b ∈ {0,1} let G_(i,b) := {y′ ∈ C : y′_k = c_k for all k ∉ J, i ∈ J, y′_i = b} (empty when i ∉ J). There are finitely many pairs (i, b), each G_(i,b) is closed (an intersection of closed coordinate conditions, or empty), and B ⊆ ⋃ G_(i,b).
 (i) By step 3, g maps A into B; by radial_map (restricted from F to A), g is (βs)-Lipschitz at x within A.
 (ii) Let (i, b) be such that y ∈ G_(i,b). Then i ∈ J, and (J ∖ {i}, c′), with c′_i := b and c′_k := c_k for k ≠ i, is a face of dimension j (c′_k = c_k = a_k for k ∈ J ∖ {i}; c′_k ∈ {0,1} for k ∉ J ∖ {i}). Its point set F′ contains y and every point of G_(i,b) ∩ B, and y ∉ La. By P(j), ψ₀ is (c₁(j)/d_a(y))-Lipschitz at y within F′ ∖ La, hence within G_(i,b) ∩ B ⊆ F′ ∖ La. By sibling lip_at_union (index type: the pairs (i, b)), ψ₀ is K₂-Lipschitz at y within B, where K₂ := c₁(j)/d_a(y) ≥ 0 (d_a(y) > 0 because y ∉ La).
 (iii) By sibling lip_at_comp (f := g, the map ψ₀ in the role of g there, K₁ := βs ≥ 0, K₂), ψ₀ ∘ g is (βs·K₂)-Lipschitz at x within A. Since ψ₀(g(x′)) = ψ₀(x′) for every x′ ∈ A, including x′ = x (step 3), ψ₀ is (βs·K₂)-Lipschitz at x within A = F ∖ La.
 (iv) The constant (printed (4)–(7), corrected). By sibling similarity_bound (with J, c, x, y, s), d_a(y) ≥ min{1/4, s·d_a(x)}; also s·d_a(x) ≤ r as in step 4. If s·d_a(x) ≥ 1/4, then d_a(y) ≥ 1/4 and βs·c₁(j)·d_a(x) ≤ β·c₁(j)·r = q·c₁(j)·(1/4) ≤ q·c₁(j)·d_a(y). Otherwise d_a(y) ≥ s·d_a(x) and βs·c₁(j)·d_a(x) ≤ q·c₁(j)·s·d_a(x) ≤ q·c₁(j)·d_a(y). In both cases, dividing by d_a(x)·d_a(y) > 0, βs·K₂ = βs·c₁(j)/d_a(y) ≤ q·c₁(j)/d_a(x) = c₁(j + 1)/d_a(x). Since the Lipschitz-at property persists when the constant is increased, ψ₀ is (c₁(j + 1)/d_a(x))-Lipschitz at x within F ∖ La. This proves P(j + 1).
6. Conclusion. By induction, P(d) holds.
